newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks seen gaining in 1997 - Reuters survey.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks seen gaining in 1997 - Reuters survey.

text.p: Mexican stocks are poised for strong, steady gains throughout the year and are likely to finish 1997 about 20 percent higher than their current levels, according to a new Reuters survey of Mexican brokerages.
Despite New Year fears that mid-term elections in July could upset Mexican financial markets, the survey shows brokers expect the blue chip IPC index of Mexican stocks to advance continually.

The survey of ten brokerage houses MXAAW, to be carried out monthly from now on by Reuters, showed an average prediction that the IPC would close 1997 at 4,575.68 points, a gain of 20.6 percent from the close on April 7.

Of the brokerages surveyed, even the least optimistic predicted a year-end level of 4,200 points for the IPC, up 10.7 percent from April 7. The most optimistic expected the Mexican bourse to climb 26.6 percent to 4,800 points.
Brokers on average expected stocks to gain a modest 0.4 percent to 3,808.45 by the end of April, in line with fallout from recent volatility on the U.S. stock and bond markets.
Three of the ten brokerages that participated in the survey actually expected share prices to fall by the end of the month.

Analysts said the main short-term stumbling block was the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting to review U.S. interest rates. Many expected a further hike to follow the 25-basis point increase in March, but were divided as to how much the bourse had already discounted the move.

Nonetheless, analysts all predicted stocks would resume a strong upward trend by the end of June -- days before the key mid-term elections in which President Ernesto Zedillo's party could lose its majority in the lower house.
The average forecast rise was of 6.4 percent to 4,037 points by June 30, above the bourse's all-time closing record of 3,938.38 points set on February 25.

Stocks were then seen advancing on average towards a new record of 4,321.08 points by the close of the third quarter of the year, despite July elections, on their way to an average 1997 close of 4,575.68.

Stock watchers interviewed by Reuters in January had believed mid-term elections were the main hurdle for the financial markets to clear, rather than tighter U.S. monetary policy to keep inflationary pressure in check. They had in general predicted the great majority of gains for the year would be chalked up in the first six months.
The IPC has risen 12.8 percent so far this year.
Mexicans will go to the polls on July 6 to renew the lower house of Congress and one-quarter of the upper house, in addition to the first-ever election of Mexico City's mayor.
